entry.title: Blade of Victory - Another fabulous platformer for the C64 by Donut 80!
entry.content:
Welcome to 'Blade of Victory', a new fantasy action-platformer from developer Donut 80. Players grab their sword and set off across eight distinct regions—ranging from blistering deserts and shadowy caverns to treacherous lakes and towering castles—in a mission to overthrow the Evil Warlock and bring peace back to the land. Along the way, you'll have to fend off a bizarre rogues' gallery of skeletons, armoured knights, ghosts, and strange winged beasts, using both sharp blade work and well-timed enemy stomps to survive. Every stage hides its own secrets and builds up to a showdown against one of eight unique bosses guarding the path to the final battle.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Players will need to gather coins and track down travelling merchants tucked away inside the levels. Managing your gold carefully is key, since those hard-earned coins can be traded for extra lives, health-boosting hearts, or score-multiplying diamonds. Knowing the right moment to hoard your cash versus spending it on vital upgrades can easily make or break a run. For C64 owners looking to test their grit, Blade of Victory offers a classic mix of exploration, combat, and old-school resource management. So yes, if this sounds like the sort of game you might enjoy, then make sure to check it out below!

entry.title: Lands of Lore AGA - Westwood's incredible PC Dungeon Crawler could be coming to the Amiga!
entry.content:
After more than six years of blood, sweat, and tears, developer Vairn has revealed a native Commodore Amiga port of Westwood Studios' classic dungeon crawler, Lands of Lore is in the works. Prompted into the final stretch after seeing fellow coder Cfou experiment with an AI-assisted port, Vairn is building Lands of Lore AGA entirely with hand-rolled C code—zero AI and zero chunky-to-planar (C2P) routines involved. Powered by the Amiga C Engine (ACE), which actually gained AGA chipset support specifically because of this project, the port converts the original PC chunky graphics, MT-32 tracks, and audio into Amiga Blitter-friendly assets, MODs, and 8SVX files. While Vairn initially got a stripped-down version running on a base machine without Fast RAM, the sheer volume of monster animations, multi-textured wallsets, and extra colours far surpasses games like Eye of the Beholder, making an 020 Amiga 1200 with 4MB of Fast RAM a firm requirement.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Lands of Lore AGA - Vairn

Although the game is already playable, Vairn notes that a few finishing touches are still needed before release, including squashing some graphical bugs, polishing the music, and wrapping up the spell system. Currently, the heavy lifting of asset conversion is handled externally via Python scripts on PC, Mac, or Linux—which crunch the data roughly 10,000 times faster than native hardware—though a standalone Amiga conversion executable is planned for the future. Even with a bit of polish left to go, Lands of Lore AGA is shaping up to be an impressive labour of love for classic Amiga RPG fans.

Links :1) Source 

Lands Of Lore AGA (EOB2 AGA update) - CFou!

In parallel to Vairn’s hand-rolled effort, veteran Amiga coder CFou!—known for his previous AGA ports of Eye of the Beholder I & II and Dune II—is also tackling a port of Lands of Lore, though he has turned to artificial intelligence to help cross the finish line on a goal he first set back in 2006. After hitting a wall with the game's complex EMC2 scripts, CFou! decided to test AI tools like Claude and Fable 5.2 to build a brand-new assembly engine from scratch, using the AI to reverse-engineer internal game logic, generate format documentation, adapt music, and build extraction tools. The resulting build already features working intros, endings, level exploration, fog, shadows, and even CD voice support via .TLK files. Yet, despite the impressive technical progress, CFou! admits the experience feels bittersweet; while he is astounded by what the AI can accomplish, he laments that his own coding skills feel increasingly obsolete, leaving him feeling more like a beta-tester than a programmer on what will likely be his final Amiga project.

Features

  • - Lands of Lore intro, ending and history animations supported (English, German and French versions)
  • - AGA Level Tester (LolLevel)
  • * F1/F2 to switch between level maps / SPACE to open or close doors
  • * Mouse and cursor controls for movement
  • * CPS/WSA/SHP/VCM/VMP/INI/INF (partial)/TIM (partial) support
  • * CD voices supported if ".TLK" files are found
  • * Sound effects, voices and music supported
  • * Map support ('C' key to see all map/'Tab' key to see and to leave map)
  • * Spell book
  • * compass support
  • * money and items
  • * Load/Save game support
  • * management of poisoning effects
  • * management of various color palettes for monsters
  • * facial animation for team members when they speak
  • * Script support: 70%
  • - Mazes, walls, fog, shadows, dialogue, level entrances and exits
  • - first quests (Roland, Thimothy, ...)
  • - key/switch/Fake wall and support
  • - item-throwing animation support
  • - traders support & money
  • - lantern & oil support (management of brightness levels, with or without lanterns)
  • - Door opening and closing animation while moving (max 5 at the same time)
  • - shadow door added when some door animations are played

entry.title: Ultracore AGA - Digital Illusions platform blaster is finally coming to the Amiga via AI/MrDig (TEST BUILD g106)
entry.content:
MrDig has announced via EAB a new project called Ultracore AGA, a work-in-progress port of the classic run-and-gun shooter. The game has a bit of a history. It originally started development for the Amiga by Digital Illusions under the name Hardcore but was sadly cancelled before completion. Decades later via Strictly Limited Games, the project was resurrected and officially released for modern platforms like the Sega Mega Drive, PlayStation, Xbox, and Nintendo Switch under the title Ultracore. Now, inspired by community discussions on the English Amiga Board (EAB), MrDig has taken on the challenge of bringing this action-packed title back to its original roots.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

[UPDATE]

The early progress on the port looks promising. A newly released gameplay video showcases the title screen and attract mode, leading into actual gameplay with full sound effects and streaming audio. The "Ultracore" build runs at stock Amiga 1200 speeds for music and sound effects with the music and effects being a Paula mix of the Mega Drive sound. The "Ultracore+" build however, requires a 68030 or better and 64 MB Fast RAM or more (about 46 MB in one block), with the original Mega Drive music and sound effects as recordings. MrDig still considers the project a work in progress but has ambitions for the final version. The target machine is an A1200 with a 68020 and 8 MB Fast RAM. Faster machines simply run smoother. In emulators (FS-UAE, WinUAE) set up an A1200 with 68020 and 8 MB Fast RAM, or a 68030 with Zorro III RAM for Ultracore+.

entry.title: Scion Ex - Seibu Denshi's 1980's Arcade shoot em up comes to the Amiga via AI/Peppe74
entry.content:
Original Arcade Version

Checking the itch io listing for new games, I've come across Peppe74's latest release of Scion Ex for the Commodore Amiga. Built with the help of AI tools, this fresh port unofficially brings Seibu Denshi’s 1984 coin-op shoot 'em up—which previously only saw a Japanese MSX home release back in 1985—to the 16-bit computer. Best of all, you won't need a heavily souped-up machine to play it, as the game is tailored to run on a stock Amiga 500 with 512K of RAM or an Amiga 1000 fitted with the A1050 front panel expansion.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

The developer notes that he opted for a classic side panel to display scores and lives so the screen would look more complete. However, redrawing that sidebar on every frame while trying to keep the dual-playfield scrolling silky smooth just wasn't doable—the frame rate took too much of a hit. Shifting the HUD to a bottom status bar turned out to be the best workaround, which explains why the gameplay area doesn't fill the entire display. Considering the game runs on a base OCS Amiga 500 with 512K of RAM, it feels like a solid trade-off for now.

In Scion Ex, you take the controls of a nimble fighter aircraft in a fast-paced, vertically scrolling battle against relentless waves of alien spaceships. Surviving the aerial dogfight is only half the job, though, as you also have to level a massive, latticed ground structure below. To pull this off, you'll need to shoot down a special mid-air vessel to unlock an extra weapon, allowing you to drop bombs onto the structure's square targets until the entire complex collapses—clearing the way to advance to the next stage and square off against the end-boss base.

entry.title: Race or Destroy - A fast top-down Amiga AGA racing game for 1 to 3 players via AI/qupe75
entry.content:
Sitting at home with a bunch of friends round for a drink then developer qupe75 might have you covered with his latest release for the Commodore Amiga called Race or Destroy. Drawing heavy inspiration from retro favorites like Super Sprint, Super Cars, and Off Road Racer, this fast-paced, single-screen top-down racer lets one to three players battle it out on the same machine using a mix of joysticks and the keyboard. You can stick to standard weapon-assisted laps, crank up the carnage in the "Race or Destroy" mode where pickups can completely wreck your rivals, or ditch the tracks altogether for last-car-standing brawls across five Destruction Derby arenas complete with sudden death overtime.


Beyond quick single races and time trials, the game has further replay value with six full championship cups—ranging from Warm Up to Ultimate—plus a custom "Own Cup" creator that supports up to eight racers at once and 20 saveable achievements. Even getting blown up doesn't mean the action stops: while a rescue helicopter hauls smashed vehicles off the asphalt, surviving drivers have to sprint for a safe zone on foot. That creates a frantic mini-game where you're desperately trying to escape on foot while rivals swerve to run you down for a bonus championship point.


Requirements

  • An AGA Amiga (A1200, A4000 or CD32 with a keyboard), PAL.
  • 2 MB chip RAM and at least 4 MB fast RAM. It uses nearly all of a stock A1200's chip RAM, so close other programs first. 8 MB fast is comfortable.
  • A hard disk. The game saves a small file in its own drawer.
  • It runs from Workbench or a Shell. It is not a WHDLoad install.

Race or Destroy was a personal feature request by the developer

entry.title: Cyclone CPC - 1984 Speccy game gets an Amstrad 128k port via NBSystems
entry.content:
ZX Spectrum Version

Forty plus years after its original 1984 debut on the ZX Spectrum, the classic helicopter rescue-em-up Cyclone has unofficially landed on the Amstrad CPC 128K thanks to developer NBSystems. Originally coded by Vortex Software co-founder Costa Panayi as a sequel to Tornado Low Level, this multidirectional action title famously skipped the CPC during the 8-bit heyday. NBSystems has stepped in to right that historical wrong, giving Amstrad owners a dedicated port packed with CPC visuals, new graphics, smoother movement, and an original soundtrack.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Amstrad CPC Version

In Cyclone CPC, players take the controls of a rescue helicopter tasked with scouring a sprawling archipelago of 14 islands to recover five crates of vital medical supplies. The catch is that a deadly, roaming cyclone threatens to tear your chopper apart at any moment, forcing pilots to balance careful navigation with urgent rescue runs. With its faithful gameplay loop and modernised Amstrad presentation, this long-overdue conversion offers CPC owners a fresh excuse to fire up their machines and check out this classic 1980's game originally by Vortex Software.

entry.title: Enter The Worlds Of Woody - Woodys World (AmigaGuru Guest Review)
entry.content:
Paul Andrews produced a remarkable number of quality games for the Amiga during the early to mid-1990s, and the crazy part is that I genuinely loved most, if not all, of them. He had a reputation for using Blitz Basic, and before you run away at the mention of it, we're talking about the developer behind titles such as Seek and Destroy (review coming soon), Overkill, and Roadkill, a game that enjoys something of a cult following today. Woody's World, however, is one of the more overlooked games in his catalogue, which is quite surprising because it is also one of the better platformers available on the Amiga. Somehow, despite its quality, it rarely gets mentioned when people discuss the system's standout platform games. That is exactly why this article is part of my The Games We Not Talk About (But Should) series. Like so many of the titles featured in this series, Woody's World is a game that deserves far more attention than it gets. Give it a proper chance and I think you'll be pleasantly surprised by just how good it actually is.




The World Of Wonder b… Umm Woody…

The first thing you'll notice about Woody's World is how good it looks and feels. While there are not that many upgrades beyond extra health, new costumes, and the occasional power-up, the game still reminds me quite a bit of James Pond 2: Robocod. Mix that with some elements from platformers like Mario and Sonic, and you'll have a pretty good idea of what to expect.

The game is packed with secret locations, most of which can only be reached by discovering hidden platforms, making tricky jumps, or navigating your way over countless traps. Exploration is heavily rewarded, and there is always the feeling that another hidden area is waiting just out of sight.

Your objective is to collect all of the chests scattered throughout the game's often massive levels (but, only 50% of them is needed to unlock the next level). There are around twenty worlds to explore, each containing three large stages. Every world features its own visual theme, or builds upon the style of the one before it, helping to keep the adventure feeling fresh as you progress.

All of the worlds are interconnected, and while there are no map screen ingame to help you find your way around, navigating the game is not nearly as straightforward as it first appears. The maps are larger and more complex than expected, which only adds to the sense of discovery and adventure that makes Woody's World such an enjoyable platformer.




Bonus Levels, Nice Hardware Trickery...

Every now and then you'll come across a bonus stage, and some of them are surprisingly original. A few feel like they could have been lifted straight out of James Pond 2: Robocod, while others introduce brand-new ideas and gameplay twists. Some of the more memorable ones have you moving at ridiculous speeds, pulling off insane jumps (you need an upgrade for that move), and relying on a fair amount of skill and precision to make it through in one piece.

Just like the main game, these bonus levels come with the added pressure of limited lives. Thankfully, extra lives are fairly common throughout the adventure, so running out is rarely a major problem. What is a problem, at least in my opinion, is the ever-present timer.

I have never been a fan of timers in platform games. I just want to relax, explore, and enjoy the levels at my own pace, and Woody's World is exactly the kind of game that encourages that style of play. With all its secrets, hidden routes, and collectibles, it feels like a game that would benefit from letting players take their time. Instead, the timer is always there, pushing you onwards whether you like it or not. It is not a dealbreaker by any means, but it is one of those design choices that always feels more frustrating than necessary.




Awesome Presentation Across The Board...

Woody's World is not without its shortcomings. It could definitely have benefited from a few big boss battles or other major set pieces to break up the gameplay. Another thing most players will probably notice is the relatively low enemy count. There are only a handful of enemies in each level, and they are often spread far apart rather than appearing in large groups.

The reason for this quickly becomes apparent when you look at what the game is doing technically. The levels are absolutely huge, packed with colourful graphics and supported by incredibly smooth multi-layered eight-way scrolling. The game also features moving platforms, rotating Mode 7-style platform sections, and plenty of visual effects that help bring the world to life. On top of that, it manages to play music and sound effects simultaneously without compromising the experience.

What makes all of this even more impressive is that Woody's World runs on a standard Amiga 500 without requiring any memory expansions (box says 1mb but it runs fine with less). That is quite uncommon for a game of this size and scope, as many similarly ambitious titles require at least ECS, additional Chip RAM, Fast RAM, or a combination of both to achieve comparable results.

When you look at the complete package, it becomes easier to understand why some compromises had to be made. The lower enemy count may disappoint players looking for constant action, but in exchange you get massive levels, fluid scrolling, impressive visual effects, and a technical showcase that pushes the humble Amiga 500 surprisingly hard.


Woodys World Box...

My copy of Woody's World is looking a little rough these days, but that's hardly surprising. It uses one of those slipcase box designs where the fit is just a bit too tight, and after more than 30 years of being taken on and off the shelf, the wear is definitely starting to show. I've even had to use a bit of transparent tape here and there to keep the box together, which is never ideal, but sometimes you have to do what you can to preserve a favourite game.

Some of you may have noticed that Woody's World was not published by Acid Software or Mindscape, unlike many of Paul Andrews' other titles. Instead, it was released by Kompart, and that may well be one of the reasons why the game ended up being relatively rare. By this point, Kompart had largely become a secondary publishing and distribution label for Richard Holmes' Black Legend Software before more or less disappearing from the scene altogether. Aside from publishing The Clue in certain regions the following year, they never really established themselves as a major Amiga publisher.

If I ever come across a sealed or mint-condition copy of Woody's World, I will happily buy it all over again. In fact, I purchased another copy around six years ago hoping for an upgrade, only to discover that it was actually in worse condition than my original one. Rather than keeping it, I sold it to my friend in Sweden. So, if you're reading this, hello Kjell Breding! At least it found a good home in the end.

Slim Findings But Still Worth It...

Woody's World comes in a traditional big box, but the contents are about as bare-bones as they come. Inside you'll find a manual and the three floppy disks that make up the game, which is really all you need. Interestingly, I seem to remember that the pirate version was spread across four disks, though I could be mistaken on that one.

One thing that has always stood out to me is the artwork used on the floppy disk labels. It looks completely different from both the cover art and the illustrations found in the manual. In fact, it is so different that I've often wondered if it was originally created for an entirely different game and simply reused here.

The strange thing is that it looks incredibly familiar. Every time I see it, I get the feeling that I've seen the character or artwork somewhere else before, but I can never quite remember where (could it be from the Pang cutscenes?). Maybe it's from another Amiga game, maybe a console title, or perhaps I'm just imagining it. Either way, it feels oddly disconnected from the rest of Woody's World's visual style, making it one of those little mysteries that has been nagging at me for years.

Summary...

Woody's World is one of those games that I genuinely think you should give a chance. It is both original and fun, especially when viewed in the context of the Amiga platform and its era. It may not have the technical wizardry of games such as Kid Chaos, Mr Nutz or Brian the Lion, but it does enough things differently to stand out from the crowd.

The learning curve can be a little rough at first, particularly when it comes to mastering the super jumps, understanding where to find upgrades and what they do, and learning how to move through the levels efficiently. Once everything clicks, however, the game becomes far more enjoyable and many of the frustrations simply fade away.

Another feature worth mentioning is the level code system. This means you do not have to complete the game in a single sitting, which is a huge bonus considering the size of the adventure and the amount of exploration involved.

Overall, Woody's World is a quality title that sadly flew under the radar for many Amiga owners. My suspicion is that it did not sell particularly well, and the fact that even used copies can be incredibly difficult to find these days certainly seems to support that theory. That is a real shame, because Vision Software produced a surprising number of quality games over the years, games that arguably deserved a much larger audience than they received.

If you are tired of hearing about the same handful of Amiga classics over and over again and want to discover something a little different, Woody's World is exactly the sort of hidden gem you should be looking for. I agree with Amiga Computing and CU Amiga, this is a 9 out of 10 game.

Screenshots courtesy of Hall of Light. GIFs and box photos by me.

entry.title: The Hobbit – They're Taking the Hobbits to Isengard in this new Amiga AGA AI Enhanced Edition by thall72!
entry.content:
Thanks to a heads up by my good friend AmigaGuru, I've been told that thall72 has just released The Hobbit – Amiga AGA Enhanced Edition. Built with the help of AI, this new port brings Melbourne House’s beloved 1982 text adventure to the Amiga 1200 and other AGA-equipped machines. Inspired by how Magnetic Scrolls classics like The Pawn and The Guild of Thieves elevated the genre on the platform, the project reimagines how J.R.R. Tolkien’s world could have looked with full 16-bit flair, albeit with AI graphics.

MSX Version


Rather than changing the core gameplay, thall72 ported the MSX version directly into native 68000 code, running it side-by-side against the original to to have total accuracy. Players will find the exact same text parser, puzzles, and independent NPCs, wrapped in a graphical AI presentation. The overhaul features a 256-colour hi-res intro and credits sequence, more than 60 new 256-colour paintings that dynamically update as the story progresses, and a brand-new victory screen. Classic Topaz text now includes a handy "press SPACE" pause so you never miss a line, while Neil Brennan’s iconic C64 disk soundtrack has been rearranged for the Amiga’s Paula chip using sampled instruments.


▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube


The release is designed to be as accessible as possible, supporting both PAL and NTSC modes out of the box alongside proper disk-saving functionality. You can grab the game either as a crazy seven-disk floppy ADF set or as a dedicated WHDLoad package for hard drive setups. To run it, you will need Kickstart 3.x and 2 MB of chip RAM, with fast RAM strongly recommended to cut down on disk swaps—or a minimum of 2 MB fast RAM if you are using WHDLoad. The port has already been thoroughly put through its paces across real NTSC A1200 hardware, MiSTer setups, and standard emulators.


AI Disclosure AI Assisted, Code, Graphics


[UPDATE] I asked the creator if it would it be possible to switch to the MSX artwork to give people a choice over AI art and the response was positive. "I will look into offering a “classic” version after the Thanksgiving holiday is over. "

entry.title: Robocop Arcade - Ranx is working on an Arcade-like version of Robocop for Amiga 500 {AI} [UPDATE]
entry.content:
The Commodore Amiga community has just been treated to a bit of a tease, with the reveal of RoboCop Arcade, a brand-new conversion of Data East’s legendary 1988 coin-op developed by Ranx with the help of AI. While the original Amiga port of the era often left fans wanting more, this  project aims to recreate the arcade game's authentic 1:1 visuals and raw gameplay feel on the humble, unexpanded Amiga 500 OCS. Built strictly around the machine's base hardware—including a stock Motorola 68000 processor and a tight 512 KB of RAM—the game aims to have hardware scrolling, Blitter-driven sprites, and all nine action-packed stages, including the iconic target-shooting bonus ranges.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Fitting an arcade-accurate experience onto a standard setup does require a lot of optimization, culminating in the entire game being packed onto a single 880 KB floppy disk. Ranx managed this through aggressive resource compression, sophisticated multi-stage loading systems, and meticulous memory management, leaving a mere 1,536 bytes of free space remaining on the disk. Amiga owners can even look forward to a classic "cracktro" sequence upon booting, alongside digitized speech and sound effects that make full use of the Amiga’s four-channel Paula audio chip. As this impressive passion project continues to evolve, the developer is actively seeking community feedback to fine-tune what is shaping up to be the definitive retro tribute to an arcade classic.

[UPDATE] A new build has been released with the following features!

  • All nine stages, including the two shooting galleries.
  • Arcade graphics at 1:1 scale, displayed in 256 × 240 pixels with 32 colours.
  • Hardware scrolling and Blitter-based graphics.
  • Music adapted to Paula’s four audio channels, with sampled speech and sound effects from the arcade.
  • A cracktro-style startup menu, including a trainer.
  • One-button and two-button joystick modes, with a separate jump button in two-button mode.
  • The entire game on one 880 KB ADF disk image.

entry.title: Champions of Krynn / Death Knights of Krynn - Classic Gold Box RPG's are reversed and bug fixed for the Amiga
entry.content:
Classic RPG fans running upgraded Amiga setups might have another reason to revisit Krynn this week thanks to a newly released reverse-engineered effort from developer mOoNsHaDo. Driven by a childhood love for SSI's classic Gold Box titles, mOoNsHaDo set out to make the Amiga port of Champions of Krynn play nicely with Kickstart 3.x, faster processors, and newer chipsets. Best of all, the updated executable now multitasks properly in the background alongside your regular Workbench apps, bringing a feeling of modernization to an incredible classic. 

The update squashes several nasty bugs that previously plagued expanded machines—even when running through WHDLoad. The patch resolves a blitter race condition on faster CPUs that used to leave bitplanes half-drawn and mess up LBM image colors, alongside an IPrefs screenmode promotion fix that stops mismatched monitor views from causing severe stretching or black screen flashing. It also clears up black flashing glitches tied to missing save games and patches out-of-bounds memory reads that caused random crashes. While this is available to download right now, mOoNsHaDo is asking players to send their save files over to marranosoft@gmail.com if they encounter bugs.

AI Disclosure AI Assisted, Code

  • This folder is a from-scratch C port of the Amiga version of Champions of Krynn written by converting, with various AIs, routine by routine, from annotated 68000 assembly decompilation

entry.title: Batman - 1986 isometric action-adventure game by Ocean Software gets a Commodore Plus/4 & C64 port
entry.content:
We haven't featured a Commodore Plus/4 game for awhile, so to change all that here's Ocean Software's 1986 classic Batman, which has finally arrived on this system as well as the C64. Originally a massive hit on the ZX Spectrum 48k, this isometric action-adventure drops players into a 3D-styled world brought to life by programmer Jon Ritman and artist Bernie Drummond. The mission remains just as tricky as you remember: explore the depths of the Batcave to track down seven scattered parts of the Batcraft hovercraft so you can rescue Robin.



▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Thanks to the efforts of Chronos from Absence and Murphy from Exceed bringing this caped crusader to the Plus/4 was no small feat. Because the Plus/4 sports a noticeably weaker CPU than the Spectrum, Murphy had to put the code through several rounds of heavy optimisation just to get the game running smoothly enough to be genuinely fun. For retro heads going back to the 80's, it will be fascinating to boot this up alongside Head Over Heels—which runs on the exact same engine—to see how the two versions stack up.

  • Released by: Absence (ACE)
  • Released by: Exceed (EXD)
  • Code by: Chronos
  • Code by: Murphy
  • Notes: AKA Batman +8 PAL/NTSC. A conversion of the ZX Spectrum classic, released for both C64 and Plus/4. The music played in the intro is Batman (short) by JCH, and the advanced frequency converter used to play it on native TED, emulates the lower notes. AI disclosure: AI assisted.

entry.title: Wizard of Wor AGA - A classic Arcade game gets an Amiga AGA edition via AI/dlfrsilver
entry.content:
Amiga owners you might like this arcade update, as if you remember playing and hopefully enjoying the 1980's Arcade game of Wizard of Wor, which also appeared on the Atari 8-bit, Atari 2600, Atari 5200, Bally Astrocade and C64. Then you'll be pleased to know that dlfrsilver has released Wizard of Wor AGA for the Commodore Amiga. A version of the game that he says, "was not only a request by a friend, but the jingles, sfx and voices can't be in chip ram (2mb of them), so you can't have the A500 loading constantly the audio as it takes too much space".

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

This port takes advantage of your system's memory, preloading all 79 digitised speech samples straight into Fast RAM while keeping the graphics, sound effects, and Paula playback buffers in Chip RAM—meaning you won't experience any annoying disk access mid-game. You don't even need an accelerator card to run it either, as the game is built for a standard 14 MHz 68020 CPU with an AGA chipset, using 2.75 MB of memory in total (1.16 MB of Chip RAM and 1.59 MB of Fast RAM, so 4 MB of Fast RAM is recommended, though a 2 MB Chip / 2 MB Fast setup should theoretically do the trick on real hardware). Once you're in, it's pure arcade nostalgia: just hit 5 to insert a coin, press 1 or 2 to jump into the action, tap F1 if you want to tweak and save your settings, or hit ESC whenever you're ready to drop back to Workbench.

entry.title: Hunter - Action/Adventure classic by Activision is getting a performance boosted Amiga RTG version
entry.content:
Let's go back in time, right back to 1991 when Activision released 'Hunter' for the Amiga and Atari ST. An action-adventure game that by today's view point would be classed as a Battlefield 4, Grand Theft Auto and Far Cry mix. Expansive, open worlds, a military theme, and the focus on small squads of soldiers or lone heroes. Well if you remember this fine game, then you'll be pleased to know that Marco-Both is working on a performance boosted Amiga RTG version. A version of the game you can see in this early footage that's been sent to us via X.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Tested on a Warp1260, the updated port bypasses the standard Amiga chipset entirely to run via Picasso96 on RTG graphics cards, shifting rendering duties from the blitter to the CPU and keeping program buffers in Fast-RAM for a dramatic speed increase. The overhaul makes the game fully system-friendly—allowing players to launch it directly from Workbench, save progress straight to the hard drive, and cleanly exit back to the operating system without rebooting. Visually, the 3D world now renders at a crisp 640x480 resolution with polygon anti-aliasing and expanded draw distances ("Far" and "Very Far") that scale the horizon and bring distant objects into view. Players can tweak these enhancements—including switching back to the classic 320x240 resolution, toggling an FPS counter, and adjusting object detail—via a built-in settings menu that saves preferences directly to a settings.ini file.

entry.title: Mirror Signal Manslaughter - A Sensible Software Grand Theft Auto mash up for the Commodore Amiga
entry.content:
Here's possibly the last Amiga news story for today and one I think you might just like! As chiptune musician and developer LukHash has unveiled Mirror Signal Manslaughter, a brand-new title for the Commodore Amiga. By blending that scrapped early-nineties pitch with the studio's signature style, LukHash has created a tongue-in-cheek tribute to one of the Amiga's greatest developers, offering a nostalgic slice of what might have been if the original lads had seen the idea through.

entry.title: Vroom - A brilliant Amiga racer from the 90's gets a performance boost via Vesuri
entry.content:
Time for some great Friday news, as developer Vesuri has released a brand-new update called Vroom Enhanced. Originally programmed by Daniel Macré and published by Lankhor in 1991, Vroom quickly earned a reputation for its simple yet addictive gameplay—even prompting Amiga Computing to joke that the fast-paced racer had turned their reviewer into a "driving freak." Now, more than three decades after its debut on the Atari ST, Amiga, and MS-DOS, this beloved speedster is getting a serious boost overhaul tailored for expanded Amiga hardware.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Real Hardware

When running on 68020+ machines, Vroom Enhanced unlocks its full original NTSC speed even on PAL setups, rendering at a silky-smooth 50 or 60 frames per second with interpolated movement between game steps. The update also cleans up the audio and controls, ensuring music and sound effects play at their proper tempo on PAL systems while eliminating annoying audio pops and clicks during the practice race. Players can now pick the Red Player’s port and input device directly from the splash window, and a long-standing bug where rapid mouse movements sent the control marble flying in the wrong direction has finally been squashed, with the installed icon automatically handling the new CUSTOM4, CUSTOM5, and CACHE settings.

entry.title: Command & Conquer - Westwood's hit strategy game for the Atari ST looks rather impressive in this 1.0 release!
entry.content:
Well this is incredible news, as indyjo has brought the classic real-time PC strategy game Command & Conquer over to the Atari ST home computer. This previously announced project is a port of Westwood Studios’ legendary 1995 title, adapting the complex strategic gameplay to a 16bit machine that first debuted in the 1980's. The true marvel of this port lies in its technical adaptation. While the original MS-DOS version relied on 256-colour VGA displays, the Atari ST hardware restricts the visuals to just 16 colours. To bridge this gap, the developer has heavily focused on precision colour reduction, translating the detailed military units and terrains into a vibrant, limited-palette art style. For retro enthusiasts and fans of 16-colour pixel aesthetics, this port promises a unique way to experience a PC gaming masterpiece.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

As noted by the website, following nearly a year of development that began with initial experiments in late 2025, Command & Conquer has officially reached its 1.0 release on the Atari ST. The conversion pulls off a remarkable technical feat by squeezing the 256-color DOS original into a complete 16-color palette via an automated asset workflow, while cutting the memory footprint in half so it can run on 4 MB of RAM—though a 16 MHz Mega STe or better is recommended for optimal performance. In a historic first for the platform, the port also features full-motion video cutscenes running at 320x200 resolution and 15 frames per second, paired with a fully digital soundtrack, speech, and sound effects supporting DMA sound, the YM-2149 chip, or a Covox Speech Thing. The developer dedicated the milestone release to the late Thorsten Otto, crediting his foundational work on the Atari ST software development ecosystem for making the project possible.

System Requirements : 

  • Minimum: Any Atari ST-compatible computer with at least 4MB of RAM.
  • Recommended: 68020+ @ 32MHz, 4MB+ RAM, DMA sound, Blitter (e.g., Atari TT).

entry.title: Wizonk! Plus - Creeping Me Out Hex Night creator 'Mixel' releases a new Amiga arena game!
entry.content:
Mixelslab—the solo developer behind Creeping Me Out: Hex Night—has just released Wizonk! Plus. Serving as a polished and expanded edition of the earlier Wizonk! Magic Arena, this colourful arcade platformer whisks players away to the kingdom of Morikar. Usually, the realm’s top spellcasters gather at Master Korath’s Flying Fortress for a no-holds-barred battle to claim the title of Master Mage. This time around, however, Witch and Wizard show up late to the party only to find the halls deserted, the other competitors vanished, and the entire stronghold crawling with monsters.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

To get to the bottom of the mystery, players can jump into a Story Mode built for solo play or two-player co-op. Taking clear inspiration from 16-bit classics like Bubble Bobble, Rod Land, and Fuzzball, this single-screen puzzle platformer tasks you with gathering gems to unlock doors across 35 stages packed with boss fights, hidden areas, and tricky enemies. The game leans heavily into retro charm that's a strong trademark with Mixel's Lab, with crisp, hand-pixeled visuals, upbeat chiptunes, a high score table, and the ability to save discovered secrets between play sessions.

When you fancy a break from saving the realm, the four-player Magic Arena mode turns up the heat with frantic, wizard-on-wizard deathmatches. You can pick from 15 distinct characters—each packing their own special weapon—and duke it out across 25 stages using an arsenal of over 25 weapons, mid-match drops, and last-minute time boosts. Best of all, almost every rule and hazard can be toggled on or off, letting you tailor the action from pure arcade chaos to a slower, more tactical scrap, complete with tournament brackets and disk-saving for ongoing rivalries. While the original Wizonk! Magic Arena remains free on itch.io and playable online via AmigaLive, Mixelslab is focusing future updates primarily on this beefed-up Plus release.

Tech Specs

  • Wizonk runs on 1MB Amigas. (512kKB+512KB A500 included!) Some features are disabled or toned down for low end systems. If you have 2MB Chip and faster CPU you’ll have more, and better quality music, as well as greater graphical detail and smoother gameplay in certain situations. (particularly in VS mode, which can get very chaotic)
  • Four Player gameplay requires a parallel port joystick adapter.

Credits

  • Design, Programming, Music, Art - Michael "Mixel" Dawes
  • Scorpion Engine - Earok
